brief.head: Paid alike, paid wrong
brief.text: Paying all civil servants in India essentially the same is “a mad idea”, Ajay Shah said: officials in rich regions are underpaid, those in poor regions overpaid. {047-C04}

brief.head: Mosquitoes are local

brief.head: The village problem

thought.who: Ajay Shah, celebrating migration as people choosing better governments

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on pushing power down
lead.head: One country, too many countries
body: India needs far more local government than it has, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah argued, in an episode that ran from mosquitoes to the Catholic Church.

Varma opened with a thought from his research for a conversation with the economist Lant Pritchett. Nation-states grew top-down, needing taxes and conscripts. City governments grew bottom-up, out of the need for order and basic services.
“What we have kind of landed up in India with is essentially just the larger coercive superstructure of the nation state with no concept of what a truly responsive government is,” he said. {047-C01}
## Mind the gaps

Shah said the place to start is heterogeneity. By CMIE survey data, average income in India’s richest region is about five times the poorest’s; for young women owning mobile phones, the gap is 10 to 15 times.
Varma added figures from Nilakantan RS: life expectancy of 75 in Kerala, 64 in Uttar Pradesh; infant mortality of seven per thousand in Kerala, 48 in Madhya Pradesh.
Then there is sheer size. Uttar Pradesh, by Varma’s own calculation, is as big as France, Germany, Italy and Spain combined, run by one state government.
“India is that diverse and that heterogeneous,” Shah said, and every question of policy must start there. {047-C02}
## Lowest level first

The rule the hosts reached for is subsidiarity: every function of government at the lowest level that can do it, Shah said. Currency belongs at the top. Mosquito control belongs in the village or the city. {047-C06}
India runs the other way. The Constitution’s concurrent list, Shah said, was meant for a wise chief minister and Jawaharlal Nehru to find a middle road. In the fine print, the Union wins.
Planners reached into the state list too, through centrally sponsored schemes that pay 65 per cent if a state runs, say, education the Union’s way. Shah would scrap them.

Cities, he argued, need a slice of GST, which can be traced to the shop where a sale happens. Of a single rate of about 10 per cent, he would give roughly three to the Union, two to the state and five to the city.
## The heretic speaks

Varma, who said there were two Ajay Shahs, demanded that the heretic present himself. The heretic celebrated migration: unhappy citizens move, and governments that drive them away lose their tax base.

Shah called the lament for migrants who left a village paradise for a city slum a luxury belief. “People choose,” he said. “And life in most urban slums is better than life in most villages.” {#slums}
Varma’s caveat was that Indian states feel the pressure only weakly, since most tax money flows to the centre.

Then Shah turned on his own side. “A chief minister in India is a little bit of a dictator,” he said, barely checked by legislatures or cowed state judiciaries. {047-C13} It is, he said, “a choice between bad and bad”.
His way out: about a hundred states, many of them cities. West Bengal could become two or three, one of them Calcutta.
Both hosts ended on cities. Varma chose Jane Jacobs’s *The Death and Life of Great American Cities*, “an absolute masterpiece”. Shah chose a book the urban thinker Bimal Patel is still building.
Varma’s sign-off: “Decentralization. Let’s do it.”

second.label: History lesson
second.head: Heaven’s org chart
second.deck: Ajay Shah traces the subsidiarity principle back to the Catholic Church
body: Economists parrot the subsidiarity principle as if it were their own, Ajay Shah said. It is older, and it comes from one of the world’s most successful organisations: the Catholic Church. {047-S06}

From around 380 to about 1950, he said, the Church was an important organisation in the world. The Vatican controlled armies and took part in international treaties, and the Church lived longer than most empires.

Empires centralised more, and tended to crash. The Church’s design secret was the opposite. Churches all over the world had their own autonomy, with the absolute minimum of central control. Over that long span, Shah said, the secret sauce was subsidiarity. {#secretsauce}

quote.text: Empires tended to crash partly because empires did more centralizing. And one of the design secrets of the Catholic Church was decentralization.

third.head: Kerala’s three-step lead
body: When COVID came, Kerala had a head start. Malayali students studying in China came home and brought the virus with them, Ajay Shah said, so the state was grappling with the first surge before almost anybody else in India. {047-S03}
Kerala has significant capabilities in its health system. It was soon up and running with quarantines, isolation and a whole bag of techniques for the early stages.

For some time, Shah said, the Union government tried to do absolutely nothing. Then it announced complete lockdowns for the entire country. Kerala’s health authorities pushed back: “We know what to do. Don’t tell us what to do. We are probably three steps ahead of you.”
Amit Varma added that Kerala’s excellent governance culture predates independence, going back decades if not centuries. {#predates}

p2.title: Where power belongs
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah, chapter by chapter, on why India must push power downwards, and the catch

sections.label: The problem
sections.head: Liberia here, Argentina there
sections.caption: India’s continental gaps
body: Start with heterogeneity, Ajay Shah said. Across India’s 3.3 million square kilometres, cultures and food habits differ, as everyone knows. The economics differs just as much.

CMIE’s household survey divides India into about a hundred homogeneous regions of roughly seven districts each. Average income in the richest is about five times that in the poorest. {047-R02} Mobile phone ownership among young women runs from 90 or 95 per cent in the best places to 5, 10 or 15 per cent in the worst.
The economist Lant Pritchett once told Shah that India’s richest place divided by its poorest gives the kind of ratio you get from Latin America’s richest place and Africa’s poorest. {047-C02}
## Country-sized states

Amit Varma brought figures from Nilakantan RS. Kerala’s life expectancy is 75, like Argentina and Thailand; Uttar Pradesh’s is 64, what you would expect from Liberia, Ethiopia and Haiti. {#lifeexp} Kerala’s infant mortality, seven per thousand, is close to the USA’s six. Madhya Pradesh’s is 48.

From Karthik Muralidharan, Varma learnt that India’s 15 biggest states would all rank among the world’s top 42 countries by population. Uttar Pradesh alone, by his own sum, is France, Germany, Italy and Spain combined. {047-S02}
~ The average district, Muralidharan points out, is bigger than 85 countries. Those countries would demand democracy, Varma said; an Indian district, with everything so centralised, cannot have it.

quote.text: Uttar Pradesh is the size of France, Germany, Italy and Spain combined. Right, it is that big.

sections.label: The state’s job
sections.head: One size fits nobody
sections.caption: mosquitoes and civil service pay
body: Heterogeneity changes two questions, Ajay Shah said: what the state should do, and how it should do it. North India may worry most about air quality, Kerala about Arabian Sea cyclones tearing at its coastline.

Amit Varma’s clearest example: Kerala has a problem of diabetes and obesity, the heartland one of malnutrition and stunting. Send both the same central policy, he said, and “people in Kerala are like WTF, this is not our problem.” {047-C03}

The how varies too. Shah called it “a mad idea” that all civil servants in India are paid essentially the same. In the rich parts, he said, they are paid a little too little; in the poor parts, too much. {047-C04}
## The mosquito question

Shah’s favourite public-health obsession is mosquitoes. Indians have given up on them, he said, but they can be controlled. {047-C05} Their characteristics change every 100 or 200 kilometres, shaped by local weather and the behaviour of their victims, so control programmes must vary by neighbourhood. Maybe Ladakh has no mosquitoes at all.
Varma heard an album title: “Mosquitoes and Ladakh”, heavy metal, in fact. {047-J02}
~ He added a figure from Karthik Muralidharan’s book: just 3 per cent of India’s budget is spent at the local level, against 50 per cent in China.

quote.text: It comes as a surprise to most people in India that actually mosquitoes can be controlled

sections.label: The principle
sections.head: Start at the bottom
sections.caption: the subsidiarity principle
body: The subsidiarity principle, Ajay Shah said, is a simple design rule: try to do each job of government at the lowest possible level, and go higher only when that fails. {047-C06} Can a village do mosquito control? Then the village should.

The European Union applies it question by question: a common currency through the European Central Bank, defence through NATO, while personal law reflects Catholic thinking in Portugal and Spain and more secular norms in the north. Its lesson, Shah said: “Don’t draw lines on maps.” {047-C07}
## Villages and cities

Amit Varma raised B.R. Ambedkar’s verdict on the village as “a sink of localism, a den of ignorance and narrow mindedness”, the basis of his case for centralising power. And what are states for? Since T20 arrived, Varma said, “states are kinda like ODIs.” {047-J06}

Shah is sceptical of villages. One of about 150 households, or 600 people, lacks the scale for enough civil servants, politicians, competition and checks and balances, and research finds the gains from village decentralisation weak. {047-C09}
~ Cities are another matter: Bombay, with a little of New Bombay, has more people than Australia. Treating the 73rd and 74th Amendments as twins, Shah said, is one reason things have not worked.

quote.text: So I’m not a romantic about village level government.

sections.label: The Indian way
sections.head: Delhi’s 65 per cent solution
sections.caption: the concurrent list and GST
body: India’s Constitution sorts the subjects of government into a Union list, a state list and a concurrent list. The concurrent list, Ajay Shah said, “is a fantasy”: its framers pictured a wise chief minister of Maharashtra finding a middle road with Jawaharlal Nehru. {#fantasy}

In the fine print, once the Union legislates on a concurrent subject, it wins. Planners then eyed the state list, through centrally sponsored schemes: run education the Union’s way and it pays 65 per cent, hijacking the state’s 35. {#sixtyfive}
Much of the Constitution, Shah observed, would be flagged by a plagiarism test as coming from the Government of India Act of 1935. {047-J10}
## Money for cities
The 73rd and 74th Amendments, pushed under Rajiv Gandhi, did not go far enough, Shah said. State finance commissions are often never set up, and lack data and neutrality when they are.

GST changes that, because each sale can be traced to a shop and so to a city. Shah’s numbers: a single rate of about 10 per cent, with roughly three to the Union, two to the state and five to the city. {047-C10}

~ Amit Varma recalled Shruti Rajagopalan’s talk on how Nehru amended the Constitution whenever he wanted to do something unconstitutional. {047-S09} A cartoon had the parliament bookshop explain that it did not stock periodicals.

quote.text: I think there should be no centrally sponsored schemes. And I think the union should vacate the concurrent list.

sections.label: The heresy
sections.head: Exit, voice and Bangalore
sections.caption: migration as exit
body: Amit Varma said there were two Ajay Shahs: a sober man of history, and a heretic whose mad ideas make sense. He demanded that the heretic present himself. {047-J11}

The heretic began with migration. In American federalism, Shah said, people who dislike their city or state move: the “exit” of Albert O Hirschman’s *Exit, Voice, and Loyalty*. Indians are used to loyalty or a little voice. {047-R16}
From James C. Scott he took the insight that early states competed not for land but for people. When a government works badly, he said, the people will leave. {047-R17}
## Against a luxury belief

Shah called the lament for migrants who left a village paradise for a city slum a luxury belief of the rich in air-conditioned rooms. Across North India, he said, an ambitious young engineer’s dream is to go to Amdavad, Bombay, Pune, Hyderabad, Bangalore or Madras. {047-C11}

Varma’s caveat: Indian states feel this competition only weakly, because only a tiny chunk of tax money comes to them. Shah’s answers were a GST slice for states and cities, and the observation that migration offsets falling birth rates in prosperous states.
~ A bee, meanwhile, kept circling Varma. “It seems to have fallen in love with me,” he said. {047-J12}

quote.text: And I rejoice and applaud the guts of the people who migrate.

sections.label: The catch
sections.head: The dictator next door
sections.caption: chief ministers and a hundred states
body: Decentralisation has a catch, Ajay Shah warned. A chief minister in India, he said, is a little bit of a dictator. Legislatures provide little check, nothing like the Rajya Sabha forces negotiation, and state judiciaries are often cowed. {047-C13}

The same logic runs through *In Service of the Republic*, his book with Vijay Kelkar: development is about dispersing power among co-equal branches that check each other, and states and cities need that as much as the Union. {047-C14}

Some advocates of handing power to the states, Shah said, seem quite comfortable with a chief minister as dictator. Amit Varma took the point as a warning against shallow thinking: decentralisation taken up as a mantra rather than reasoned from first principles.
## The way out

Shah’s fixes include a GST slice for cities, separate thinking for cities and villages, political reform in states and cities, and an intellectual community for every government. Strip out the knowledge, he said, and government becomes a raw power project. {047-C16}
His thumb rule is about a hundred states, many of them cities. {047-C15} West Bengal could be two or three, one of them Calcutta, dealing directly with the Finance Commission.
~ That fits the present Constitution, Shah said, which matters when drafting skills are poor and amendments are fraught with difficulty.

quote.text: If you get the checks and balances, if you get a sensible republic, then the economic growth will inevitably follow.

side.boxText: *In Service of the Republic*, by Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah, argues that development is about dispersing power: co-equal executive, legislative and judicial branches that check each other. India’s failures, it says, come from an overbearing, concentrated Union. {047-R23}

contQuote.text: Every state requires a commensurate intellectual community. You need the data sets, the thinkers, the research papers, the public debate, the criticism. Without that no government ever works well.

p3.deck: A dog, two cats, a Dutch tank battalion and the mayors who became ministers

stories.caption: Susan Thomas and the dog bite
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a dog bite, a government clinic and Kerala
stories.head: A bite, and no needless needles
body: Susan Thomas was bitten by the family dog. She always apologises that it was her fault, Ajay Shah said: she was troubling the dog. Susan, he explained, has very high standards for good behaviour.
What followed, in Kerala, was a list of surprises. Amit Varma suggested they began with the biting.

Surprise number one: the family took her to a government clinic. In most of India, Shah said, people like them would go to a private establishment. In Kerala there was no friction; it was the obvious thing to do.
Surprise number two: the doctor was there. The facility was not vacant, and he was smart, competent and sensible.
He asked the correct questions. Is it a family dog? Is the dog at home and fine? Will it be under observation? Then he gave her a little antiseptic and sent her home. {#antiseptic}

If the dog had rabies, Shah explained, it would collapse and go crazy first, and that would be the time to start vaccinating the human. Most doctors in India, private or public, would instead “blast” a course of rabies vaccination.
In most states, he said, the family would not think of a government facility, which would most likely be vacant, or staffed by “a low quality hack” who would blast nine injections.
~ The moral, for Shah, was India’s immense diversity. “I may be radical in my views on the health system,” he said, “but I respect what Kerala has in a government run health system.”
stories.why: Policy cannot be one size fits all, Shah argued, when state capacity itself varies so much. Radical reform for most of India’s government health system should still leave alone what Kerala has built. {047-S04}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s own doctor, Lancelot Pinto, saw him through COVID twice on paracetamol and cough syrup. {047-S05}

stories.start: So the fable of the monkey and the two cats is like this
stories.end: how much of the funds are actually going to the states
stories.caption: the monkey and the two cats
stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells Pranay Kotasthane’s fable
stories.head: Split the bread, keep the bread
body: Two cats find a piece of bread under a table at the same moment and fight over it. A canny old monkey in a tree offers to mediate and make equal pieces.

He breaks the bread, but one half is bigger, so he eats a bit of it. Too much: now the other half is bigger. He keeps going until two tiny equal bits remain, then takes those too, as payment for his labour. {047-S08}

Amit Varma had the fable from a newsletter post by Pranay Kotasthane. {047-R12} Its point: Indian states fight over horizontal devolution, which state gets what share, and talk too little about vertical devolution, how much reaches the states at all.
~ The South complains that it contributes more than the North, Varma said, while the centre gives only 42 per cent to the states.
stories.why: While the states quarrel over their shares, the bigger question goes unasked: how much of the bread the centre keeps. For real decentralisation, on Kotasthane’s argument, the vertical split matters more than the horizontal one.
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah noted that the episode now had “a dog, a cat, a monkey”. Varma added: “And tanks, many, many tanks.” {047-J08}

stories.start: So uh in Netherlands uh at some point uh they were buying German tanks
stories.end: That is the dream of uh the European Union
stories.caption: the Dutch tanks
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah, unable to resist, on the Dutch army
stories.head: Dutch money, German command
body: Ajay Shah said he could not resist talking about tanks. Amit Varma sighed: “You can never resist talking about tanks.” {047-J03}
After the Second World War, Shah said, the Netherlands decided to let it go that Germany had invaded it a couple of times, and went back to buying German tanks. {047-J04}

But a small NATO member with perhaps twenty tanks found that running its own logistics tail and maintenance was silly at that scale. So it told the Germans: “We’ll pay for the tanks, but the tanks will be controlled by the German army on our behalf.” Dutch soldiers served in units fully integrated into the German army. {047-S07}
~ Arrangements like this, Shah said, have taken place all over Europe.
stories.why: Instead of defining the state by lines on maps, Shah argued, decide each function at the scale where it works: one currency, shared defence, pooled tanks and local personal law. {047-C07}
stories.postscript: Varma pictured a thumbnail of Shah peering out of a tank, and ended the episode: “Ajay in a tank.”

stories.start: And the interesting uh thing to note is that in our
stories.end: colonial coercive superstructure we you know we lost that little part of the
stories.caption: the freedom fighters as city bosses
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the freedom movement’s apprenticeship
stories.head: Salem first, then the nation
body: Not so long ago, Amit Varma said, India had empowered mayors. C. Rajagopalachari was effectively mayor of Salem in 1917, as chairman of the municipal board. {#salem} Jawaharlal Nehru held a similar position in Allahabad in 1923.
Chittaranjan Das held it in Calcutta, and then Subhas Chandra Bose. Sardar Patel, Varma said, was prominent in the Allahabad municipal council.

Under the British, local governments were empowered to do local tasks that the colonial government could not be bothered with, and they trained future leaders. Those who became prime minister and home minister, Varma said, did not simply go from activists to politicians. “They knew governance, they cared deeply about it, they understood public finance.” {047-S01}
~ After independence, he said, India kept most of the colonial coercive superstructure and lost that little part of the puzzle.
stories.why: Running cities was where the freedom movement’s leaders learnt governance and public finance. In losing empowered local government, Varma suggested, India lost the crucible out of which its first prime minister and home minister emerged.

quiz.q: Which four European countries, combined, match Uttar Pradesh’s population by Amit Varma’s own calculation?
quiz.a: France, Germany, Italy and Spain, all run by a single state government.

quiz.q: What does the subsidiarity principle say, and which institution did Ajay Shah trace it to?
quiz.a: Place each function at the lowest workable level; the Catholic Church practised it for centuries.

quiz.q: Why did the Kerala doctor give Susan Thomas only antiseptic after the dog bite?
quiz.a: A rabid dog would collapse first; that would be the time to vaccinate.

quiz.q: In Pranay Kotasthane’s fable, what does the monkey finally take as payment for his labour?
quiz.a: The last two tiny, equal bits of bread, after eating the rest himself.

quiz.q: How would Ajay Shah split a single-rate GST of about 10 per cent?
quiz.a: Roughly three per cent to the Union, two to the state, five to the city.

quiz.q: Between Test cricket and T20, what did Amit Varma say states were like?
quiz.a: ODIs, the middle format that people said was no longer needed.
